# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are rising globally [1]. The dominant rationale for mechanical exclusion of the left atrial appendage (LAA) rests on observations that the appendage is the principal site of thrombus formation in non-rheumatic AF. In a foundational study, of 1288 patients with non-rheumatic atrial fibrillation, 221 (17%) had thrombus detected, and of those with atrial thrombus, 201 (91%) had it located within the left atrial appendage [2]. During AF the appendage fails to contract effectively, producing blood stasis that predisposes to thrombosis [2]. These insights, together with the bleeding burden of lifelong anticoagulation, motivated the development of percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) as a site-specific, nonpharmacologic alternative for stroke prevention.

## Pivotal Randomized Trials Versus Warfarin

The PROTECT AF trial provided the first randomized evidence. Patients (n=707) with nonvalvular AF and at least one risk factor were randomized 2:1 to the Watchman device or continued warfarin; after device implantation, warfarin was continued for about 45 days, followed by clopidogrel for 4.5 months and lifelong aspirin [3]. LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but an early periprocedural safety hazard was identified [3,4].

PREVAIL was designed to confirm these findings with newer operators. It was a multicenter, 2:1-randomized controlled trial that enrolled 282 patients with nonvalvular AF and a CHADS2 score ≥2, randomized to the Watchman device or continued warfarin [5]. At 18 months, the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve prespecified noninferiority, with a rate ratio of 1.07, an outcome attributed to an unusually low event rate in the warfarin group [5,6]. Importantly, early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF [5]. The 5-year outcomes of PREVAIL combined with those of PROTECT AF demonstrated that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke [7]. A pooled net-clinical-benefit analysis reinforced this: the upfront risk of periprocedural events is counterbalanced over time by reduced bleeding events and mortality [8].

## Patients Unsuitable for Anticoagulation

Because the randomized trials enrolled only warfarin-eligible patients, the ASAP study addressed those with contraindications. This multicenter, prospective, nonrandomized study evaluated LAA closure with the Watchman device in 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and a CHADS2 score ≥1 considered ineligible for warfarin [9]. The findings suggested LAAC could be performed safely without a warfarin transition [9]. The confirmatory randomized ASAP-TOO trial, however, was terminated due to slow enrollment, leaving guidance reliant on nonrandomized evidence for this population [10].

## Comparison With Direct Oral Anticoagulants

As DOACs became standard, head-to-head data were needed. PRAGUE-17 was a multicenter, randomized, noninferiority trial comparing LAAC with DOACs in patients with nonvalvular AF who had a history of bleeding, a cardioembolic event on anticoagulation, and/or a CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HAS-BLED >2 [11]. In long-term (4-year) follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [12].

The OPTION trial extended this comparison to patients undergoing AF ablation. Wazni and colleagues, for the OPTION Trial Investigators, reported on left atrial appendage closure after ablation for atrial fibrillation [13]. LAAC resulted in significantly less bleeding than oral anticoagulation; at 36 months a primary safety event had occurred in 8.5% of the LAAC group versus 18.1% of the anticoagulation group, with comparable efficacy [13].

## Device Evolution and Comparative Performance

A next-generation device was evaluated in PINNACLE FLX. The primary safety endpoint was met with a low adverse event rate of 0.5%, the primary effectiveness endpoint was met with a 100% rate of effective closure at 12 months, and the implant success rate was 98.8% [14]. The Amulet IDE trial provided the first large head-to-head device comparison. The Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [15]. Real-world performance has been confirmed in the NCDR LAAO Registry [16].

## Complications: Device-Related Thrombus

Device-related thrombus (DRT) is an important adverse outcome, since thrombus may form on the left atrial face of the device and embolize [17]. In a large pooled analysis of Watchman cohorts, Dukkipati and colleagues characterized its incidence, predictors, and prognostic implications [17], and meta-analyses confirm DRT is associated with substantially higher ischemic event rates [18].

## Surgical Context

The LAA can also be excluded surgically. In LAAOS III, 4811 patients with AF and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 2 undergoing cardiac surgery for another indication were enrolled [19]. Ischemic stroke or systemic embolism was documented in 4.8% of the occlusion group versus 7.0% of the no-occlusion group (hazard ratio 0.67), on a background of continued anticoagulation [19,20].

## Guidelines and Conclusions

Contemporary guidelines now incorporate LAAC for selected patients. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline and the 2024 ESC/EACTS guidelines address percutaneous and surgical LAA occlusion as options for stroke prevention, particularly in patients with contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [21,22]. Percutaneous LAAC has matured from an investigational concept into a guideline-endorsed therapy, supported by randomized comparisons against both warfarin and DOACs [3,5,11], iterative device improvements [14,15], and growing registry experience [16]. Key uncertainties remain—including optimal antithrombotic regimens, management of peridevice leak and DRT, and outcomes in anticoagulation-ineligible patients—motivating ongoing trials [10,13]. References [23]–[30] provide additional supporting literature on procedural safety, anatomy, registries, and antithrombotic management referenced throughout the LAAC evidence base.
